narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 68.4% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess risk, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year in law school was the strongest influence, pushing the model strongly toward predicting failure. Standing in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) is far below the average of accepted students, who typically rank around the middle of their class. Your first-year class rank was the third most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure; again, you placed in the lowest decile while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile.

Your LSAT score worked in the opposite direction. At 34 it is below the 37.2 average of accepted students, yet the model still treated this score as a modest positive signal that slightly increased the chance you would pass. However, this encouraging factor was not nearly enough to offset the two weak academic performance signals.

Taken together, the model concluded that your academic standing in law school raised the risk of bar exam failure too high for admission. To improve your chances next time, focus on raising your class ranking through targeted study support or tutoring, and consider retaking the LSAT if you can realistically raise your score. These steps would directly address the factors that most hurt your current prediction. (248 words)
